title: $400K to Live Comfortably on H-1B? What 10 US Cities Actually Cost in 2026
excerpt: Entrepreneur Aniruddha Anjana's viral breakdown estimates a family of four needs $407,597 a year in San Francisco and $204,672 in Houston to live comfortably in 2026 — personal estimates that expose how fast a six-figure H-1B salary disappears.
body:
• Entrepreneur Aniruddha Anjana, who spent a decade working in the US, has estimated the annual household income a family of four needs to live comfortably in 10 major US cities in 2026 — San Francisco tops the list at $407,597, Houston is the lowest at $204,672.
  • The math uses the 50/30/20 budgeting rule: 50% for fixed expenses like rent, taxes and childcare, 30% for discretionary spending such as travel and entertainment, and 20% for investments.
  • What it means for you: if you are on an H-1B visa weighing a US move with a family, these are personal estimates of what "comfortable" costs — they are not visa minimums. A $150,000 offer that looks like ₹1.25 crore-plus back home can still fall short of the comfort bar in coastal tech hubs, where housing and childcare alone can consume half the paycheck.
  • The figures are one person's calculation, not official H-1B salary requirements or financial advice — but they expose how fast a six-figure American salary disappears once a family starts paying American living costs.

The $400,000 Reality Check

For Indian professionals, an H-1B visa has long been shorthand for a better life in the United States. A widely shared breakdown by an Indian-origin entrepreneur is now putting an uncomfortable number on what that life actually costs: in San Francisco, a family of four would need about $407,597 a year to live what he calls a comfortable lifestyle in 2026.

Aniruddha Anjana, who spent a decade working in the US and now runs a startup from India, shared the estimates on his Instagram account @growwith_ani, and the analysis has been picked up by NDTV Profit, American Bazaar Online and Times Now World. His calculation assumes two adults and two children and applies the popular 50/30/20 budgeting framework: 50 percent of income for fixed living expenses, 30 percent for discretionary spending, and 20 percent set aside for long-term investments.

San Jose follows San Francisco at approximately $402,771, with Boston at $368,742. New York comes in at $337,875, Seattle at $334,131 and Washington, D.C. at $319,405. Even in cities considered more affordable, the bar is high: Chicago at $242,278, Austin at $229,050, Dallas at $214,490 and Houston at $204,672.

"What it means for you: if you are on an H-1B visa weighing a US move with a family, these are personal estimates of what "comfortable" costs — they are not visa minimums."

Context & Background

The estimates land at a moment when the economics of the H-1B route are under unusual scrutiny: on October 8, the Trump administration suspended green-card processing at Microsoft, Adobe and six major IT services firms, freezing the H-1B-to-green-card pipeline at some of the largest employers of Indian professionals.

Anjana's argument, as reported by American Bazaar Online, is that many H-1B holders — particularly those outside the top-paying tier of big tech — earn salaries that look strong in dollar terms but fall short of his comfort benchmarks once housing, healthcare, childcare, transportation, taxes and everyday expenses are counted. As he puts it, even cities viewed as affordable can require a household income above $200,000 for a family of four.

Impact & Analysis

The numbers are striking because they invert the usual diaspora math. A ₹1 crore salary sounds transformative in India; $150,000 sounds transformative in a US job offer letter. But in the Bay Area, the median rent for a family-sized apartment alone can run $4,000–$5,000 a month, full-time childcare for two children can exceed $3,000 a month, and federal plus state taxes take a large first bite. Under Anjana's framework, half of a $407,597 income — about $204,000 — goes to fixed costs, which is precisely why the headline number looks so large.

Two caveats matter. First, these are personal estimates, not official figures: the H-1B program's actual salary floors are set by Labor Department prevailing-wage levels for specific occupations and locations, and USCIS does not require a family-of-four "comfort" threshold. Second, the 50/30/20 rule is a savings-forward framework — a family can live in San Francisco on less, but with thinner discretionary spending and slower savings. The value of the exercise is honesty: it prices the lifestyle, not just the survival.

For prospective movers, the practical read is comparative. The spread between San Francisco ($407,597) and Houston ($204,672) is nearly two-to-one, which means the same job at the same company can feel like a different economic life depending on the office zip code. That gap is worth pricing into any relocation decision — or any negotiation.

What's Next

The conversation Anjana started is unlikely to fade, because the underlying pressures are not fading: US housing costs remain elevated, childcare is expensive everywhere, and immigration policy is adding new fees and uncertainty to the H-1B path. For Indian families plotting a move in 2026, the takeaway is to run the household budget before accepting the offer — and to remember that the dollar figure on the offer letter is the beginning of the calculation, not the end.
